props.title: The Little Mermaid
props.initialSlug: A whole new world under the sea.

sections.content: The Little Mermaid (1989) marked Disney Animation's triumphant return to form, launching the Disney Renaissance that defined a generation. After struggles with The Black Cauldron (1985) and Oliver & Company (1988), the studio took a massive creative risk by returning to the classic fairy tale musical format. Howard Ashman and Alan Menken's Broadway-style songs transformed animation storytelling, with "Part of Your World" establishing the "I Want" song template that would influence everything from Beauty and the Beast (1991) to Frozen (2013).

sections.content: The film's technical innovations were groundbreaking. Glen Keane's fluid character animation of Ariel set new standards, particularly in the "Part of Your World" sequence where her hair flows underwater. The multiplane camera techniques created unprecedented depth, while the integration of CAPS (Computer Animation Production System) for digital coloring marked the last Disney film to use hand-painted cels. These advances influenced Pocahontas (1995) and Tarzan (1999).

Ursula stands as one of Disney's most memorable villains, inspired by drag queen Divine and performed with scene-stealing gusto by Pat Carroll. Her character design and "Poor Unfortunate Souls" number created the template for theatrical Disney villains, directly influencing Scar in The Lion King (1994) and Dr. Facilier in The Princess and the Frog (2009). sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond Disney. Its success proved audiences would embrace musical animation with complex themes, paving the way for films like Anastasia (1997) and The Prince of Egypt (1998). The character of Ariel - active, rebellious, and driven - helped reshape princess narratives, influencing characters from Mulan (1998) to Moana (2016).
